title: The NY Subway Vigilante
summary: Hosts examine the 1984 New York subway shooting by Bernard Getz, who shot four young men on a Manhattan-bound 2 train in December 1984 after they approached him asking for five dollars. The episode covers the context of crime-ridden 1980s New York, Getz's 1981 mugging and gun permit denials, his flight to New Hampshire and surrender, public reaction and media coverage, the 1987 criminal trial where he was acquitted of attempted murder and other serious charges but convicted of illegal gun possession, the 1996 civil suit in which a jury awarded Darryl Cabey $43 million, and the later fates of the victims and Getz. Also includes a listener mail segment about Camp David's location.

entities.name: Fear and Fury: The Reagan Eighties, The Bernard Goetz Shootings and The Rebirth of White Rage

segments.title: Opening and introduction to Bernard Getz
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the subway vigilante Bernard Getz, who shot four teens on a New York subway in 1984, and mention Five Bullets by Elliott Williams and the media attention the case received.

segments.title: The shooting and the teens' background
segments.summary: Overview of the December 1984 shooting on the 2 train: four young men approached Getz, one asked for five dollars, and Getz shot each of them, leaving Darryl Cabey paralyzed. Hosts discuss the teens' ages and whether they were armed, and note Al Sharpton's comments that they were no angels.

segments.title: New York City in the 1980s
segments.summary: Discussion of 1980s New York as a city near bankruptcy with high crime, subway lawlessness (about 38 crimes a day on the subway), and the sense of constant alertness among residents.

segments.title: Public reaction and support for Getz
segments.summary: Getz became a folk hero; surveys showed support across racial lines, Joan Rivers sent a telegram, and merchandise appeared. Critics included Jimmy Breslin and Mayor Ed Koch, who condemned vigilantism.

segments.title: Getz's surrender in New Hampshire
segments.summary: After fleeing on foot and by rental car, Getz went to New Hampshire, was identified from a sketch, and turned himself in to the Concord Police Department, speaking candidly to police and the NYPD.

segments.title: Getz's background and 1981 mugging
segments.summary: Getz was an electrical engineer who calibrated equipment and was loner-like. In 1981 he was mugged in a subway station by three Black men, which led him to seek a gun; NYC denied his permit and his appeal, and he bought a gun in Florida.

segments.title: Getz's statements and the gun
segments.summary: Quotes from Getz's police interview about wanting to maim the youths and running out of bullets; he had five bullets in a six-shot revolver. Getz's contradictory statements are discussed.

segments.title: Indictment and grand jury proceedings
segments.summary: A first grand jury in January 1985 indicted only on illegal weapons possession; a second grand jury in March 1985 indicted on murder, assault, and other charges.

segments.title: Dismissal and appeal
segments.summary: Thirteen counts were thrown out over alleged poor grand jury instructions and perjury; an appeals court reinstated the case in 1986.

segments.title: Details of the train encounter
segments.summary: Account of the confrontation: Canty approached Getz, the request for five bucks, Getz unzipping his windbreaker, five shots fired in about twenty seconds, and the disputed final shot into Cabey's spine.

segments.title: Disputed facts: robbery intent and screwdrivers
segments.summary: Debate about whether the teens intended to rob Getz, the screwdrivers in their pockets, their history of stealing from arcade games, and Breslin's interview with Cabey. Discusses New York self-defense law allowing deadly force if one reasonably believed a robbery was imminent.

segments.title: 1987 criminal trial
segments.summary: Criminal trial ran from December 1986 to June 1987, with jury selection taking four months. Canty testified under immunity, Allen pleaded the Fifth, and Ramseur refused to testify and was held in contempt. Eyewitness testimony and expert testimony from neuropsychiatrist Bernard Yudowitz and ballistics expert Joseph Quirk were presented; a subway car tour was held.

segments.title: Verdict and sentence
segments.summary: Getz was acquitted of attempted murder, assault, and reckless endangerment, and found guilty only of illegal firearm possession. He received about 250 days in prison, and probation was revoked.

segments.title: 1996 civil trial and aftermath
segments.summary: Darryl Cabey filed a civil suit in 1996; the jury found for Cabey and awarded $43 million. Getz filed for bankruptcy and Cabey never collected. Getz testified, expressing no remorse.

segments.title: Later life of Getz and the victims
segments.summary: Getz still lives in his West Village apartment, ran for mayor in 2001 and for public advocate in 2005, was arrested in 2013 for attempting to sell drugs to an undercover officer, and became a pro-marijuana advocate. Cabey was paralyzed; Canty and Allen were in prison; Ramseur died of an overdose in 2011.

segments.title: Further reading
segments.summary: Hosts recommend Five Bullets by Elliott Williams and Fear and Fury by Heather Ann Thompson, debating the colon in the title.

segments.title: Listener mail: Camp David
segments.summary: Listener Rachel from Raleigh wrote that she and her fiancé both thought Camp David was in Texas; the hosts respond and invite listener emails.
